title: With dignity
hookLine: zakat is the right of the poor, not a favor, and given with respect

lines: A COUNTER, A CLIPBOARD, A LINE.
cards: A woman stands at the counter of a food pantry. The volunteer is kind, but there's a clipboard, a line of people behind her, and a question asked loud enough for the line to hear. She gets the bag.
She also gets the feeling of having been looked at. Nobody did anything wrong, exactly. And yet she walks out smaller than she walked in.
The Qur'an has a word about this moment, and it isn't about the food. It's about who the food belonged to before it changed hands.

teach.h: A DUE SHARE: HAQQ, A RIGHT.
teach.b: Start with the word the Qur'an uses. In surah fifty-one, describing people of faith, Pickthall's translation says: "And in their wealth the beggar and the outcast had due share."
The Arabic word is haqq: a right, something owed. Surah seventy says it again: the wealth of the faithful holds "a right acknowledged" for the one who asks and the one who goes without.
So in this way of seeing it, the giver isn't doing the poor a favor. Their share was already inside the giver's money. Zakat hands it over.
Second, if it's their right, how it's given matters.

teach.h: A KIND WORD BEATS A WOUNDING GIFT.
teach.b: Surah two is direct: "A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury." The next verse warns believers not to make their almsgiving worthless by reminding people of it, or by hurting them.
Giving and then lording it over someone empties the gift. Third, the text praises giving that stays hidden.

Surah two says giving openly is good, but giving in secret to the poor is better for you. Some teachers connect this to the person receiving: when nobody watches, nobody is shamed. Fourth, the counter itself.
Life can put anyone on either side of it.
The one holding the bag of groceries is asked to remember they're returning something, not bestowing it.

teach.h: AND IN THEIR WEALTH THE BEGGAR AND THE OUTCAST HAD DUE SHARE.
teach.b: That changes the voice you use, where you stand, whether you make someone wait in front of a crowd. So the woman at the pantry, in this reading, is not a charity case. She's collecting what was hers.

how: Muslim teachers describe zakat as the poor's due rather than a favor, and stress giving it without reminders, public display or wounding words.

o: giving only to people who have earned your respect
giving generously so others see and follow your example
zakat given as a right owed, quietly, without reminders

p: the beggar and the outcast had due share
a kind word beats a wounding gift
better for you, says surah two

s: in the Qur'an's words, the poor have a due share in the wealth of the faithful
"and in their wealth the beggar and the outcast had due share" (51:19).
once the gift is given, reminding someone of it doesn't matter
surah two warns that reminders and hurt make almsgiving worthless.
the Qur'an only praises giving that others can see
it calls open giving good, and giving in secret to the poor better for you.

games.q: you've just helped a neighbor pay a bill. a friend asks what you've been up to this week. what does surah two point toward?
o: tell the story, so others are inspired to give.
say nothing about it, and let the gift stay quiet.
mention it to the neighbor, so they remember.
games.why: the text warns against making a gift worthless with reminders, and calls giving in secret better. silence protects the one who received.

practice: Bring to mind the last time you gave something to someone who needed it, money, food, a ride, your time, and replay it slowly: where you stood, whether you looked them in the eye, whether you mentioned it afterward.
No verdict, just notice. Then picture the next time, done as if you were handing over something already theirs, and if you pray, hold that person in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: With dignity. Zakat given as a right owed, haqq, not as a favor, and without reminders or wounds. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a right, a due, something owed; the word for the poor's share in the wealth of others.

carryVoice: Your line: their right. Given quietly, with a kind word, and never mentioned again. See you tomorrow.
